etymology: Old English nawther, nāhwæther: not whether, not either of two. Webster 1828: not either; not the one nor the other; a negative that refers to persons, things, or clauses, ordinarily paired with nor. The KJV uses it to shut both doors: not this, and not that.
biblical_def: Neither in Scripture is a double refusal. It does not leave a third option for the sinner to invent. The commandment is fenced on both sides: Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it (Deut 4:2). The prayer of Agur will not choose either ditch: give me neither poverty nor riches (Prov 30:8). Our Lord binds forgiveness the same way: if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (Matt 6:15). Laodicea is condemned for occupying the excluded middle: thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot (Rev 3:16). Galatians 3:28 is the soteriological form of the same word, not an anthropological one: there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus. That oneness is union with Christ in justification and adoption. It does not unmake Jew and Gentile as peoples in providence, nor bond and free as stations in this age, nor male and female as the creational pair of Genesis 1:27. The dictionary therefore reads neither as Scripture’s way of closing a pair: no adding and no subtracting; no unforgiveness that still claims the Father’s pardon; no lukewarm third temperature; no second ground of birth besides God. What God has shut with neither is not reopened by a modern “both/and.”
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NEITHER as not either; not the one nor the other. It refers to persons or things, to clauses of a sentence, and by usage to any number considered individually. It is ordinarily followed by nor.
webster_full: NEITHER, n. / pron. adj. — Not either; not the one nor the other. It refers to individual things or persons. The upright judge inclines to neither party.

NEITHER, conj. — In the first part of a negative sentence, followed by nor in the subsequent part. It is neither the one nor the other. Webster notes the KJV pattern: Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it (Gen 3:3).
NEITHER, pron. — Primarily two; by usage any number, referring to individuals separately considered.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
Proverbs 30:8
Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
Matthew 6:15
But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
Revelation 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Galatians 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Neither is corrupted when Galatians 3:28 is conscripted to erase male and female, when lukewarmness is rebranded as nuance, and when the double fence around the Word (neither add nor diminish) is replaced by a living document that does both.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is the androgynous reading of Galatians 3:28. Progressive evangelical and queer-theological registers treat neither male nor female as the abolition of sexed creation. Paul is not rewriting Genesis 1:27. He is naming who is justified: the ground of standing in Christ is not pedigree, station, or sex. Creational order remains. Complementarian headship and male-only eldership are not repealed by a verse about union with Christ. The recovery is to keep soteriological unity and creational distinction in the same Bible.

The second corruption is Laodicean branding. Neither cold nor hot is now sold as balance, complexity, and refusing to be “extreme.” Christ calls it vomit. The church that will not confess, will not discipline, and will not burn is not sophisticated. She is lukewarm. The recovery is the Lord’s own wish: cold or hot — not the excluded middle.

The third corruption is to add and diminish at once. Deuteronomy 4:2 shuts both gates. Higher criticism diminishes — Moses denied the Torah, Paul denied the Pastorals, Daniel pushed into the Maccabean age. Magisterial accretion and progressive “new light” add. Both refuse the neither. The Reformed confession keeps the 66-book canon as sufficient: nothing to add as binding, nothing to subtract as obsolete.
roots_summary: Old English nawther / nāhwæther, not either of two. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek oude (G3761) at Matt 6:15; Greek oute (G3777) at Rev 3:16; Greek ou (G3756) at Gal 3:28. Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:8 are untagged for the English word neither in this cache; no Hebrew number is invented for them.
roots_lines: Greek oude (G3761) — not even, neither, nor (Matt 6:15, neither will your Father forgive).
Greek oute (G3777) — and not, neither, nor (Rev 3:16, neither cold nor hot).
Greek ou (G3756) — no, not (Gal 3:28, there is neither Jew nor Greek — the cache tags the negative particle, not a separate “neither” root invented for every English occurrence).
Old English nawther — not whether; not either of two.
usage: Neither shuts both doors: do not add, and do not diminish; do not refuse to forgive, and then claim the Father’s pardon.
Laodicea is neither cold nor hot — the excluded middle is not wisdom; it is vomit.
Galatians 3:28 is oneness in Christ, not the erasure of male and female as creational sexes.

etymology: From accord: Latin ad + cor, heart, then Old French acorder, to bring heart to heart, to agree. Webster 1828: agreeing, harmonizing; suitable, in accordance with; always followed by to; never a bare preposition. The KJV’s ordinary theological phrase is according to — measured by a standard that is not the speaker.
biblical_def: According in Scripture names the rule something is measured by. Salvation is not according to us: Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace (2 Tim 1:9). Election has the same meter: the called are those who love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose (Rom 8:28); we were predestinated according to the good pleasure of his will (Eph 1:5). Sanctification has a written rule: Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word (Ps 119:9). Judgment has a written rule too: the dead are judged according to their works (Rev 20:12). The word therefore refuses two modern instincts at once. It will not let the sinner be saved according to his record, and it will not let the saint walk according to his feelings. Grace elects according to purpose; the Word cleanses according to itself; the last day renders according to deeds. Those are not three religions. They are one God, measuring three moments by three of His own standards — purpose, Word, and works as evidence — never by the sinner’s self-report.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ACCORDING as agreeing, harmonizing; suitable, agreeable, in accordance with. It has its true participial sense, agreeing, and is always followed by to. It is never a preposition.
webster_full: ACCORDING, p.pr. — Agreeing; harmonizing. Th’ according music of a well mixt state.

ACCORDING, p.pr. — Suitable; agreeable; in accordance with. Our zeal should be according to knowledge. Webster insists the word agrees with a sentence, is always followed by to, and is never a preposition.
scriptures: Romans 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Ephesians 1:5
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
2 Timothy 1:9
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,
Psalm 119:9
Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.
Revelation 20:12

And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
corruption_summary: According is corrupted when “my truth” and private self-report replace God’s purpose and Word as the measure, when election is recast as according to foreseen faith, and when cheap grace pretends the last day will not judge according to works as evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: The age’s favorite standard is the self. “Live according to your truth.” “According to my story.” Scripture will not take that meter. A young man cleanses his way according to the Word, not according to the heart (Ps 119:9; Jer 17:9). The recovery is to restore the object of to: purpose, good pleasure, Word, mercy — God’s, not ours.

The second corruption is synergistic election. Semi-Pelagian and decisionist schemes make calling according to foreseen faith or according to the sinner’s yes. Second Timothy 1:9 shuts that door: not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace, given in Christ Jesus before the world began. Conditional election is not a humble reading of Romans 8:28. It is a different according-to.

The third corruption is antinomian abuse of the same grace. If salvation is not according to works, the flesh concludes that the last day will not be according to works either. Revelation 20:12 forbids that. Justification is by imputed righteousness, received by faith alone. Judgment still opens books. Works are not the ground of acceptance; they are the public evidence of what grace made. Rome confuses the two and justifies by works. Cheap grace confuses the two and empties the books. The Reformed confession keeps both texts.
roots_summary: From accord (Latin ad + cor, heart; Old French acorder). Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek kata (G2596) at Rom 8:28, Eph 1:5, 2 Tim 1:9, Rev 20:12. Psalm 119:9 tags Hebrew dābār (H1697) on thy word, not a separate Hebrew for English according; no number is invented for the English prepositional phrase.
roots_lines: Greek kata (G2596) — down from, according to, after (Rom 8:28; Eph 1:5; 2 Tim 1:9; Rev 20:12).
Hebrew dābār (H1697) — word, matter (Ps 119:9, according to thy word — tagged on the noun, not invented as a Hebrew for the English participle).
English according to — Webster: participial, always with to; the KJV’s ordinary meter-phrase for purpose, Word, grace, and judgment.
usage: Called according to his purpose — election’s meter is God’s good pleasure, not the sinner’s record.
Cleanse the way according to thy word — the standard is written, not felt.
The dead are judged according to their works — evidence at the last day, not a second gospel.

etymology: Past participle of burn, Old English beornan / bærnan: to be on fire, to consume with fire. Webster 1828: consumed, scorched, heated, subjected to the action of fire. In the KJV the ordinary sacred cluster is the burnt offering / burnt sacrifice — the whole given to the flame. The companion entry burnt-offering treats the institution; this page is the participle and the KJV word burnt itself.
biblical_def: Burnt in Scripture is fire that finishes the gift. Noah’s first altar after the flood is this: he offered burnt offerings on the altar (Gen 8:20). The law’s first offering is the same: the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD (Lev 1:9). Abraham is told to offer Isaac for a burnt offering (Gen 22:2) — the whole son, not a portion — and the ram is provided in his stead. The Hebrew name of the rite is already treated at burnt-offering; the English participle tells the manner: nothing held back from the flame. That is why the prophets can say God is full of burnt offerings when the heart is not His (Isa 1:11), and why Samuel can say to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). Hebrews reads the whole Levitical flame as shadow: In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure (Heb 10:6), because the body of Christ is the offering God did appoint. Psalm 51 holds both ends without cheating: the broken spirit now, and the restored altar later — thou delightest not in burnt offering while the bones are still unhealed (Ps 51:16), yet burnt offering returns when Zion is built. The dictionary therefore refuses two reductions. Burnt is not a mood of exhaustion, and it is not a technique for buying God. It is whole consumption, fulfilled in the Son who gave Himself an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour (Eph 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BURNT as the participle passive of burn: consumed; scorched; heated; subjected to the action of fire.
webster_full: BURNT, p.p. of burn. — Consumed; scorched; heated; subjected to the action of fire.
scriptures: Leviticus 1:9
But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD.
Genesis 22:2

And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
Psalm 51:16
For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.
Hebrews 10:6
In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure.
Isaiah 1:11

To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats.
corruption_summary: Burnt is corrupted when the whole-offering is recast as burnout and self-care, when ritual fire is treated as a bribe that excuses disobedience, and when the cross is reduced to inspirational self-gift without penal substitution.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic English has stolen the participle and aimed it at the nerves. “Burnt out.” “Burned.” The recovery is not to deny exhaustion as a creaturely limit; it is to refuse the swap. Leviticus 1 is not a wellness crash. It is a whole animal on a real altar, a sweet savour unto the LORD. The church that talks more about burnout than about burnt offering has changed religions.

The second corruption is ritualism without obedience. Isaiah 1 and 1 Samuel 15 already named it: God is full of burnt offerings when the hands are full of blood and the ears are shut. High-church aesthetic, low-church busywork, and every scheme that treats giving, singing, or attending as a substitute for repentance repeat Saul at Gilgal. To obey is better than sacrifice. The flame does not launder rebellion.

The third corruption is to empty Hebrews 10. Liberal Protestantism makes the burnt offerings a primitive stage the race outgrew; some evangelical registers make the cross a display of love without wrath, a self-gift without substitution. The epistle says the contrary: God had no pleasure in those offerings because He prepared a body for the Son. The burnt thing is fulfilled, not discarded, in Christ’s once-for-all offering. Penal substitution is not a later theory laid on the text. It is why the fire had to finish the gift.

Leviticus 1:9 and Genesis 22:2 are untagged in this cache; no Hebrew number is invented for them. roots_lines: Hebrew ‘ōlāh (H5930) — burnt offering, that which goes up in smoke (Ps 51:16; Isa 1:11).
Greek holokautōma (G3646) — whole burnt offering (Heb 10:6, In burnt offerings … thou hast had no pleasure).
Old English beornan / bærnan — to be on fire; the English participle the KJV uses for what the flame finished.
Companion entry burnt-offering already holds the rite; this page is the participle burnt, not a newly guessed Strong’s for every untagged OT occurrence.
usage: A burnt sacrifice is the whole given to the flame — Noah after the flood, the law at the door of the tent, Isaac named and the ram provided.
God may be full of burnt offerings and still refuse them when the heart is shut (Isa 1:11; 1 Sam 15:22).
Hebrews 10:6 reads the Levitical flame as shadow; the body of Christ is the offering God appointed.
